tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
This worktree holds your open PR to `entireio/cli`. It's been waiting on review for a while and is now a long way behind main.

**PR #2028:** [docs(agent): complete `DeclaredCaps` exclusion list](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2028), from `MuskanPaliwal:fix-declared-caps-builtins`

**What it does** (two real commits; everything else is merges from main):
- `b39fd12aa` filled in the doc comment above `DeclaredCaps` in `cmd/entire/cli/agent/capabilities.go`. That comment lists the built-in capabilities that have no external-protocol flag, and it had drifted out of date.
- `52374d422` followed up on Soph's review by turning that list into a rule the build enforces:
  - Every `As*` helper now resolves through either `builtinCapability[T]` or `declaredCapability[T]`. Four helpers were changed to fit, with no change in behavior: `AsSidecarImageProvider`, `AsStreamingTextGenerator`, `AsContextInjector` and `AsModelLister`. A fifth, `AsPermissionConfigOwner`, now also goes through `builtinCapability`, which adds a nil check it didn't have before.
  - A new test in `architecture_test.go` reads the package source and fails if a helper uses any other pattern, or if the documented list doesn't exactly match the `builtinCapability` helpers in alphabetical order.

**Review history:** Soph checked the original list against the source, confirmed the additions and suggested enforcing it with an automated test. You built that and have asked twice for another look. No formal review yet, and status is `REVIEW_REQUIRED`.

**Current state:**
- The local branch matches your fork. No Entire Trail is linked to this branch.
- GitHub shows the PR as **CONFLICTING**. Upstream main is about 1,236 commits ahead, last fetched 2026-10-12.
- The conflict is only in `capabilities.go`: main rewrote the same doc comment to add `HomeScopedInventoryExtractor`.

**Rebasing alone won't be enough.** Main has added helpers that the new test will catch:
- `AsStaleHookReporter` uses `builtinCapability`, so it fits. It just needs adding to the list, along with `HomeScopedInventoryExtractor`.
- `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` use a third pattern: built-in only, and they actively reject external agents. The test as written would flag both as using an unsupported pattern.

So getting the PR merge-ready means merging upstream main, resolving the doc comment, and deciding how to handle that third pattern. Two options:
- Add a third standard function for it, such as `builtinOnlyCapability`, and teach the test about it.
- Exempt those two helpers from the check.

I haven't changed anything. Want me to propose the merge and test update in detail?

content.text:
Here's how I'd get PR #2028 merge-ready.

## The problem
The PR conflicts with upstream main, and main has changed the code the new test checks. If we only fix the conflict, the test will fail.

## Why (checked against `upstream/main`)
1. **Text conflict.** Main changed the same `DeclaredCaps` doc comment in `capabilities.go` to add `HomeScopedInventoryExtractor`. That's the only file with a conflict.
2. **New built-in helpers the list doesn't have yet:** `StaleHookReporter`, `HomeScopedInventoryExtractor`, `HomeLayoutProvider` (in `home_layout.go`) and `TaskTranscriptMatcher` (in `task_transcript.go`). All four already use `builtinCapability`. The test would report the list as out of sync, which is the drift it exists to catch.
3. **A third pattern the test doesn't allow.** `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` are built-in only, and they also reject any `CapabilityDeclarer` agent. Their bodies are hand-written, so the test would fail with "must return builtinCapability[T] or declaredCapability[T]". Switching them to `builtinCapability` would remove that rejection, so that's not an option.

## Proposed change
1. **Merge `upstream/main` into the branch**, as the branch already does, so no force-push is needed. Rewrite the doc comment as one sorted list. Your branch already converts the five helpers that main still has in the old style.
2. **Run the agent package tests on the merged tree first** to confirm they fail for causes 2 and 3 exactly as described.
3. **Add a third resolver, `builtinOnlyCapability[T]`,** next to the other two in `capabilities.go`. It does a type assertion and then refuses any agent that implements `CapabilityDeclarer`. Rewrite the two helpers to use it, with no change in behavior.
4. **Teach the test about it.** Count `builtinOnlyCapability` as a third standard resolver. The documented list becomes every capability with no `DeclaredCaps` field: both built-in kinds, 22 entries after the merge.
5. **Verify:** focused `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/...`, then `mise run check`.
6. **Then, each with your approval of the exact text:** push to your fork, update the PR description (the test now covers three resolvers and the list has grown), and optionally post a short comment to Soph.

## Alternative
Leave the two helpers alone and give the test a named exemption list. It's a smaller diff, but it brings back the hand-maintained list this PR is meant to remove. Each new built-in-only helper would mean editing that exemption list, so it would drift again the same way.

**I recommend the new resolver.** It keeps the PR to one idea: every helper uses a standard resolver and the list is checked automatically. It also removes two hand-written copies of the same logic. The cost is that the PR now changes two more helpers, which is worth calling out to the reviewer.

I'd do this in this worktree, since it's already the PR's branch. Moving it under `work open 2028` can wait until after it's merged or skipped. Okay to go ahead with the recommended option?

The audit is back. The merge subagent is still running.

**What the audit confirms on upstream main:**
- There are 32 `As*` helpers. 18 use `builtinCapability`, 9 use `declaredCapability`, and 5 have hand-written bodies.
- 4 of those 5 are the ones your branch already converts: `AsSidecarImageProvider`, `AsContextInjector`, `AsModelLister` and `AsPermissionConfigOwner`, plus `AsStreamingTextGenerator`, which is `declaredCapability` written out by hand.
- That leaves two helpers outside both resolvers: `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource`. These are the ones the proposed `builtinOnlyCapability` would cover.

**Two things to know about those two:**
- **The rejection of external agents never actually fires today.** The only external-agent type (`*wrappedAgent`) implements neither interface, and `DeclaredCaps` has no field for them. Keeping the rejection is still right, because it guards against future changes. It just means the new resolver changes no real behavior.
- **`AsLateTranscriptWriter` has no tests at all.** Its external-agent rejection is completely untested. `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` is covered by `TestAsOutOfBandTokenSource` at `capabilities_test.go:456`, including the external-agent case. In the follow-up I'd add a matching test for `AsLateTranscriptWriter` before switching it to the new resolver, so the switch is checked against a test that already passes.

I'll report when the merge finishes.

content.text:
`AsLateTranscriptWriter` checks whether an agent writes its transcript file only *after* a turn ends. If it does, the function hands that agent back so the caller can use its special methods. Otherwise it returns `false` and the caller uses the normal code path.

**What "late transcript writer" means**

Most agents, like Claude Code, add lines to their transcript file during the turn. When Entire's Stop hook fires, the file already holds the full turn.

Some agents only write the file after the Stop hook. Today the only one is Antigravity (`agent/antigravity/transcript.go`). For these agents, two things can look like bugs but aren't:
- Partway through a turn, the file on disk only holds earlier turns, so an empty or stale transcript is expected. Entire should carry on with less data rather than fail.
- A transcript position recorded at Stop can lag if the agent's write hasn't landed yet.

The interface (`agent.go:280`) also requires two methods that use the agent's own way of counting lines:
- `CountTranscriptPosition(content)`: where the transcript currently ends. This is stored as the checkpoint's start offset.
- `SliceTranscriptFromPosition(content, start)`: return only the content after that offset.

These matter because the writer and the readers must count lines the same way. A blank line counted differently would make the next checkpoint start reading from the wrong place.

**Example caller** (`attach_transcript.go:120`):

```go
if lw, ok := agent.AsLateTranscriptWriter(ag); ok {
    return lw.SliceTranscriptFromPosition(data, start) // agent's own counting rule
}
return transcript.SliceFromLine(data, start)          // generic line slicing
```

The other callers are in the strategy layer (condensation and hooks). They use it to decide whether an empty live transcript should be tolerated instead of treated as an error.

**What the helper itself does** (`capabilities.go:168`):
1. A nil agent returns `false`.
2. If the agent doesn't implement `LateTranscriptWriter`, it returns `false`.
3. If the agent is an external agent (one that implements `CapabilityDeclarer`), it returns `false` anyway. The external protocol has no way to express this trait, and `DeclaredCaps` has no field for it, so only built-in agents can have it.
4. Otherwise it returns the agent and `true`.

Step 3 is what makes it different from `builtinCapability`, which would skip that check. That's why the plan adds a separate `builtinOnlyCapability` rather than reusing `builtinCapability`. As the audit found, step 3 never triggers today, because the external agent wrapper doesn't implement these methods. It's a safeguard in case that changes.

content.text:
Because those two helpers follow a rule that neither existing function expresses, and the test only accepts helpers that use a standard function.

**The three rules side by side**

| Agent | `builtinCapability` | `declaredCapability` | The two helpers today |
|---|---|---|---|
| Built-in agent that implements T | yes | yes | yes |
| External agent that implements T | **yes** | only if its `DeclaredCaps` field is true | **always no** |

`AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource` are built-in only *and* refuse external agents. Neither function does that, so their bodies are hand-written. Your test then flags them: "must return builtinCapability[T] or declaredCapability[T]".

**Why not just switch them to `builtinCapability`?** That changes behavior. External agents would get through instead of being refused. It doesn't matter for real agents today, but there's concrete evidence it would break something: `TestAsOutOfBandTokenSource`'s subtest "capability declarer excluded" (`capabilities_test.go:483`) uses a mock that is an external agent *and* implements the interface, and expects `false`. That subtest would fail.

**So `builtinOnlyCapability[T]`:**
- gives that third rule a name;
- removes the two hand-written copies;
- lets the test treat it as a third allowed function.

That keeps "every helper uses a standard function" true with no behavior change.

**A simpler option I should have mentioned:** the existing function already produces the same result if no `DeclaredCaps` field can ever be true:

```go
return declaredCapability[LateTranscriptWriter](ag, func(DeclaredCaps) bool { return false })
```

- Built-in agent: returns `true`.
- External agent: asks its declarations, gets `false`.

That's identical behavior, with no new function and no change to the resolver check.

**Downsides of that option:**
- `return false` reads like a trick unless a comment explains it.
- The list test would group these with the external-protocol capabilities, so they'd drop out of the doc list. Fixing that means teaching the test to spot the always-false check, which is more fragile than matching a function name.

**I still recommend `builtinOnlyCapability`.** It says what it means at the call site, and keeps the test as a simple name match. The `return false` option has the smaller diff, if you'd rather not add new code to the agent package in this PR. Which do you prefer?

content.text:
Think of each `As*` helper as a door, with a guard deciding who gets through. There are two kinds of agents: **built-in** ones, which Entire ships, and **external** ones, which are plugins.

Right now the code has two standard guards:
1. **`builtinCapability`**: "Can you do this job? Then come in." Built-in and external agents are treated the same.
2. **`declaredCapability`**: "Can you do this job? If you're external, show me your permission slip." The slip is `DeclaredCaps`.

Two doors, `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource`, need a third rule:
3. "Built-in agents only. External agents never get in, slip or not."

No standard guard does that, so those two doors have a hand-written guard. Your PR's test says every door must use a standard guard, so it fails on them.

**Fix options:**
- **Use guard 1 anyway:** wrong. It would let external agents in, and an existing test would catch that.
- **Use guard 2 with a slip that can never say yes** (`return false`): same result, but it's a trick. A reader has to stop and work out that "permission slip that's always no" really means "built-in only".
- **Make guard 3, `builtinOnlyCapability`:** its name says exactly what it does. The test can then just check "is this one of the three standard guards?"

So I'm recommending it mainly for clarity: the rule gets a plain name instead of being hidden in a trick or copied by hand into two places.

The cost is one small new function, about 8 lines, in the agent package. If you'd rather this PR add nothing new, the "always no" option works too; it's just less obvious to read.

content.text:
The full check is still running in the background. Here's why these functions exist.

**The problem they solve**

Entire works with many coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, and plugin agents). They don't all support the same features. For example:
- Some can count token usage; others can't.
- Some can generate text; others can't.
- Antigravity writes its transcript late; Claude Code doesn't.

So all over the codebase, Entire needs to ask "can *this* agent do X?" before using that feature.

**How Go answers that**

Each feature is an *interface*, a set of methods. Go lets you check whether a value has those methods:

```go
tc, ok := ag.(TokenCalculator)  // "does this agent have the token methods?"
```

The `As*` helpers wrap that check so callers write one line, `agent.AsTokenCalculator(ag)`, instead of repeating the logic everywhere.

**Why a plain check isn't enough for plugin agents**

Built-in agents are simple: if Claude Code has the methods, it supports the feature.

Plugin (external) agents are different. Entire wraps every plugin in one Go type, `wrappedAgent`, which forwards calls to the plugin program. That wrapper has the methods for many features whether or not the plugin behind it actually supports them. So "does it have the methods?" always says yes, which tells you nothing.

That's why plugins send a list of what they really support, `DeclaredCaps` (the permission slip from before). Hence the three functions:

| Function | Question it asks | Used when |
|---|---|---|
| `builtinCapability` | Does it have the methods? | The feature can't be reached by plugins anyway, so the method check is enough |
| `declaredCapability` | Does it have the methods, and if it's a plugin, did it declare support? | The plugin protocol supports this feature |
| `builtinOnlyCapability` | Does it have the methods, and is it *not* a plugin? | The feature must never be used through a plugin |

**Why your PR matters**

Before, each helper did this check by hand, slightly differently each time. Some forgot the nil check (`AsPermissionConfigOwner`), and the doc list of "no plugin declaration" features kept falling out of date.

Your PR makes every helper use one of these three functions, and adds a test that reads the code to keep the doc list accurate. If someone adds a new helper and forgets the list or the standard pattern, the build fails instead of a reviewer having to notice.

I'll report back when `mise run check` finishes.

**Proposed PR description for step 3.** It isn't posted; I'll update the PR only after you approve this exact text:

---

`DeclaredCaps` keeps a list of the capabilities that built-in agents can have without declaring them through `DeclaredCapabilities`. That list had fallen out of date more than once: the original doc comment missed several helpers, and capabilities added later (`ToolInvocationScanner`, then `StaleHookReporter`, `HomeLayoutProvider`, `TaskTranscriptMatcher`) were not added to it.

This PR adds a test that enforces the list, so reviewers no longer have to keep it in sync by hand.

## What changed

Every package-level `As*` capability helper now resolves through one of three standard functions:

- `builtinCapability`: built-in capabilities that need no declaration
- `builtinOnlyCapability`: built-in capabilities that external (`CapabilityDeclarer`) agents must never get, even if they implement the interface
- `declaredCapability`: capabilities gated by `DeclaredCaps`

`builtinOnlyCapability` replaces two hand-written copies of the same logic in `AsLateTranscriptWriter` and `AsOutOfBandTokenSource`. The `SidecarImageProvider`, `StreamingTextGenerator`, `ContextInjector`, `ModelLister`, and `PermissionConfigOwner` helpers were moved onto the standard functions without changing their signatures.

A package-wide AST test scans the production files of the top-level `agent` package and checks that:

- every `As*` helper uses one of the three standard functions;
- the capabilities resolved through `builtinCapability` or `builtinOnlyCapability` exactly match the list documented above `DeclaredCaps` (now 22 entries);
- the documented list is sorted alphabetically.

## Compatibility

There are no public API or protocol-schema changes. The changed helpers return the same values and keep the same declaration gating. The one difference is that `AsPermissionConfigOwner` now returns false for a nil agent, the same as every other helper.

## Verification

- `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/agent/...` passes.
- `TestAsLateTranscriptWriter` was added before the refactor, including the case where an external agent must be refused. It passed on the old code and still passes after the switch. Previously this helper had no tests.
- Removing `LateTranscriptWriter` from the documented list makes the architecture test fail with the expected out-of-sync error.
- Lint is clean. Locally, two integration tests (`TestManualCommit_MidSessionRebaseFollowsHead`, `TestCheckpointDelete_LeftoverDeletedIDNeverReceivesNewWork`) fail the same way on unmodified `main` and appear to be environment-specific; CI covers them.

---
